UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
) 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
) 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
 
 
PRE-CONFERENCE STATEMENT OF MASON EMNETT 
ON BEHALF OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
 
 
Pursuant to the Commission’s July 2, 2026 notice in the above-captioned proceeding,1 and 
on behalf of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (Constellation), Mason Emnett submits this 
pre-conference statement addressing potential PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) stakeholder and 
governance reforms in advance of the Commissioner-led technical conference to be held on 
July 23, 2026.  
I. 
COMMENTS 
Policymakers and stakeholders have been discussing potential improvements to PJM’s 
stakeholder process and governance structure for years.2  The intensity of this debate has ebbed 
and flowed over time but appears to be reaching a high point, with particular focus on how states 
can more effectively participate in PJM’s decision-making and whether PJM is organizationally 
 
1 PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Second Supplemental Notice of Commission-Led Technical 
Conference, Docket No. AD26-7-000 (July 2, 2026).  
2 See, e.g., Members Committee, Stakeholder Process Super Forum, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (Aug. 22, 2019), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mc/20190926/20190926-item-01-
stakeholder-process-super-forum-presentation.ashx (a concentrated effort to make adjustments to the stakeholder 
process to help address prioritization and transparency); Stakeholder Process Forum, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 
https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/forums/stakeholder-process-forum (PJM has a regular, monthly 
“check-in” to address issues that come up in the stakeholder process, the Stakeholder Process Forum, where all 
stakeholders, including representatives of state commissions and agencies, are welcome to participate); Open Letter 
to the PJM Board of Managers from Nine Governors re: Board Vacancies (July 16, 2025), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2025/20250717-nine-governors-letter-regarding-board-
vacancies.pdf; ICYMI: In Philadelphia, Governor Shapiro Convenes Historic PJM Summit to Push for Reform, 
Lower Energy Costs, and Protect Grid Reliability, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (Sept. 23, 2025), 
https://www.pa.gov/governor/newsroom/2025-press-releases/icymi--in-philadelphia--governor-shapiro-convenes-
historic-pjm-s.

2 
 
capable of quickly responding to emerging resource adequacy challenges.  In response, the 
Commission initiated this proceeding to “focus on identifying and evaluating actionable reforms 
to improve PJM’s ability to address system needs in a timely and efficient manner.”3  An effective 
stakeholder process is critical in PJM and, as elaborated below, changes can and should be made 
to ensure transparency and an opportunity for all voices to be heard.  However, these or any other 
changes considered must preserve PJM’s independence as a regional transmission organization 
(RTO) and maintain consistency with the Federal Power Act (FPA).   
It is also critical that the Commission, PJM, the states, and stakeholders identify with 
precision the problems (from their respective perspective) that need to be solved so that we can 
collectively debate solutions that actually address each issue.  For example, some suggest that 
PJM’s lack of section 205 filing rights results in gridlock when PJM’s Members cannot find 
consensus on a complicated issue.  Yet most of the unrest in PJM over the last decade has involved 
issues related to resource adequacy, generator retirements and replacements, and capacity market 
rules changes—matters over which PJM already has section 205 filing rights and is able to take 
action under section 205 even when the Membership disagrees.  When PJM has delayed action, it 
has been because its leadership has decided not to proceed, not because of any lack of authority.  
In the same vein, PJM’s lack of section 205 rights over energy market issues has not deterred 
PJM’s action under section 206 when its leadership decided to proceed without Membership 
endorsement.4  PJM has sufficient authority under its existing decisional structure to take action 
when its leadership concludes that action is necessary.  Strong and decisive leadership by PJM, 
 
3 PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Notice of Commission-Led Technical Conference, Docket No. AD26-
7-000 (May 12, 2026). 
4 See, e.g., Facilitating PJM Independent 205 Filing Rights Over Transmission Planning of PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C., Docket No. EL24-119-000, at 9-11 (June 21, 2024) (filing by PJM under section 206 of the FPA); Enhanced 
Price Formation in Reserve Markets of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL19-58-000, at 1 & n.1 (Mar. 29, 
2019) (filing by PJM under section 206 of the FPA).

3 
 
whether proceeding under section 205 or section 206, is what matters, and the Commission, states, 
and stakeholders should be focused on improvements to the stakeholder process or governance 
mechanics that reinforce (rather than undermine) PJM’s leadership.  
A. The Role of States: Existing Participation and Additional Opportunities 
Much of the current debate regarding the effectiveness of the PJM stakeholder process and 
related governance mechanics appears to be driven by concerns from some states that they do not 
have sufficient opportunity to be heard by PJM or otherwise participate in PJM processes and 
decision-making.  Notwithstanding these concerns, state representatives have a long history of 
active participation in PJM’s stakeholder processes, both individually and collectively.  For 
example, state representatives can and routinely do: 
• Submit issues charges for PJM and its Members to consider;5   
• Participate directly in the stakeholder process, such as by submitting proposals and 
weighing in on others’ proposals6 (and, in fact, state-supported proposals have been 
 
5 See, e.g., Issue Charge, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (July 16, 2025), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mrc/2025/20250723/20250723-item-05---3-revised-sub-annual-
auction-issue-charge---clean.pdf (sub-annual issue charge brought by Governor Josh Shapiro, on behalf of the 
Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, which led to the creation of the Sub-Annual Capacity Market Senior Task Force, 
https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/task-forces/sacmstf); Clean Attribute Procurement Senior Task Force, 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/closed-groups/capstf (this now-closed 
group was established by an issue charge to coordinate the PJM markets with state clean energy attributes).   
6 See, e.g., Appendix 1, attached below (compiling written submissions by PJM state entities in two recent PJM 
Critical Issues Fast Path stakeholder processes); Letter from Maryland Delegate Lorig Charkoudian on behalf of the 
National Caucus of Environmental Legislators (NCEL), to President Mills & the PJM Board (June 23, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-written-comments---
maryland-delegate-lorig-charkoudian-on-behalf-of-ncel.pdf; Agenda for Critical Issue Fast Path (CIFP) - Reliability 
Backstop Procurement (RBP) / Connect & Manage (C&M), PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., (June 30, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-agenda.pdf 
(Maryland State Senator Katie Fry Hester allotted time for comments).

4 
 
selected by PJM and its stakeholders—and accepted by the Commission—as the 
path forward7); 
• Submit letters to the PJM Board expressing their views directly to the PJM Board;8 
and 
• Participate in state-specific task forces, user groups, and committees.9 
States are nevertheless expressing increasing concern that participation has been difficult 
and ineffective. To enhance the ability of states to participate consistently in PJM processes, OPSI 
has begun expanding its capabilities so it can more effectively coordinate and represent state 
interests.  The Commission, PJM, and its Members should support this right-sizing of OPSI 
resources to ensure that the organization is sufficiently staffed and supported (including by lawyers 
and consultants) and capable of enabling a robust and effective state/PJM relationship, particularly 
as states seek to address the resource adequacy challenges that have been the focus of recent state 
concern. 
 
7 See 2025 Periodic Review of Variable Resource Requirement Curve Shape and Key Parameters of PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-455-000, at 7-8 (Nov. 7, 2025) (describing the Joint PJM/PA Public 
Utility Commission, Vice Chair Barrow proposal that received super-majority support from stakeholders and was 
adopted by the PJM Board without modification), accepted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 194 FERC ¶ 61,049, on 
reh’g, 196 FERC ¶ 61,007 (2026). 
8 In just the past year-and-a-half, the PJM states, in some capacity, have submitted over fifty letters to the PJM 
Board on a variety of issues.  See Appendix 2, attached below.  In addition, the Organization of PJM States, Inc. 
(OPSI) can meet with the PJM Board multiple times annually. 
9 See, e.g., Independent State Agencies Committee, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., https://www.pjm.com/committees-
and-groups/state-commissions/isac (focused primarily on transmission matters); Affordability and Reliability for 
Residential Consumers User Group, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-
groups/user-groups/arrcug (includes state-appointed consumer advocates of several restructured states within the 
PJM service area); Public Interest & Environmental Organizations User Group, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 
https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/user-groups/pieoug (includes representatives of Consumer Advocates, 
as well as public interest and environmental organizations, and holds an annual meeting with the PJM Board); Clean 
Attribute Procurement Senior Task Force, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-
groups/closed-groups/capstf (this now-closed group was set up to “coordinate a comprehensive discussion” between 
OPSI, PJM stakeholders, and staff “around enhancements to enable states and other willing buyers to procure clean 
resource attributes, on a voluntary basis, through a regional and centralized procurement or market.”).

5 
 
PJM also could facilitate more effective engagement by the states by being explicit 
regarding the input that it seeks from states and the forum(s) in which that input is to be provided.  
Whether accurate or not, there is a general perception that PJM leadership does not take input from 
the states seriously.  PJM can correct that perception by identifying in a structured way the specific 
input that it desires from states, where and when that input is to be provided, and then 
communicating back to the states how that information was considered by PJM to reach decisions.  
Constellation recommends that PJM do this for the following topics at a minimum: 
• Proposed changes to market rules and planning processes; 
• Jurisdictional authority of PJM relative to the states; 
• Load forecasting, including obtaining input from state retail regulatory authorities 
on what large load requests are sufficiently real to be included in PJM’s capacity 
procurement and transmission planning; 
• Resource adequacy preferences, including whether the state intends to rely on PJM 
markets for capacity procurement or to establish its own planning and procurement 
mechanism(s) and whether the state prefers certain capacity types and, if so, how 
those resources should be procured;10 and 
• Views on the relative importance of rule or process changes so PJM can factor that 
into its workload prioritization.  
 
10 See Transcript of Technical Video Conference at 225, Technical Conference Regarding Resource Adequacy in the 
Evolving Electricity Sector, Docket No. AD21-10-000 (Mar. 23, 2021) (Jason Stanek, Chairman, Maryland Public 
Service Commission: “So [FRR] would allow us to reclaim resource adequacy. But at the same time we’ve been 
relatively content in the capacity markets up until the Calpine decision, and we’d like to stay if possible.”); 
Transcript of Technical Conference at 179-247 (Panel 3), Meeting the Challenge of Resource Adequacy in Regional 
Transmission Organization and Independent System Operator Regions, Docket No. AD25-7-000 (June 4, 2025), 
(roundtable discussion with state public utility commissioners and other state representatives about the role of states 
in resource adequacy in PJM).

6 
 
This increased collaboration also should go both ways.  There are a number of market and 
resource adequacy-related matters governed by state laws and regulations that are impacted by 
PJM decisions or otherwise interact with the wholesale markets and planning functions overseen 
by PJM.  PJM should work with the states to identify the areas of support they need to fulfill their 
own duties.  This could include matters ranging from the siting and permitting of transmission, 
generation, and gas pipeline infrastructure necessary to bring PJM-planned resources online, to 
opportunities to increase the use of bilateral contracting and hedging structures to protect 
consumers from wholesale market volatility.   
As noted above, effective coordination with the states will require both PJM and the states 
to be specific as to the information or input to be provided and the forum(s) in which that 
information and input is to be provided.  To ensure that OPSI can provide meaningful and 
coordinated support to the states in meeting those expectations, PJM should: 
• Establish protocols and schedules for meeting regularly with state commissions and 
their staff, both individually and collectively, to seek input regarding important 
market and transmission issues, rule changes, and other areas of concern, including 
both staff-to-staff and leadership-to-leadership meetings;  
• Establish a process for states, both individually and collectively, to request and 
receive technical information and support on matters related to wholesale markets 
and/or infrastructure planning and their interactions with state regulation and retail 
rates; and 
• Develop (with Commission and state guidance) options for additional hedging 
tools, such as a state purchasing authority (or buyers’ cooperative), to facilitate

7 
 
bilateral contracting11 and manage consumer risks associated with wholesale price 
volatility.12 
Finally, PJM also should discuss with OPSI and the PJM Governors Collaborative whether 
they desire to establish an organization, either separate from or integrated with OPSI, to facilitate 
participation by state elected officials in PJM processes.  Elected officials do not currently have a 
forum similar to OPSI to support their engagement in PJM matters and may lack the technical 
resources needed to engage effectively.  Additional funding for such an organization, whether 
separate from or integrated with OPSI, could be provided through the PJM Tariff to ensure 
sufficient staffing and support (including by lawyers and consultants).  This could be accomplished 
through an amendment to Schedule 9 of the PJM Tariff, which already provides funding for both 
OPSI as well as the Consumer Advocates of PJM States, Inc. (CAPS). 
B. The Commission’s Role: Ensuring PJM Processes Are Effective 
In situations where the Commission desires to see prompt action on a particular matter, or 
the Commission is concerned that a lack of stakeholder consensus is leading to inaction by PJM, 
the Commission can spur action by using its convening authority, both informal and formal.  For 
example, the Commission could hold conferences/workshops on enhancing bilateral transactions 
or other steps that PJM could take in coordination with states to protect consumers from price 
volatility in the wholesale market.  Despite the best efforts of PJM and its stakeholders, 
 
11 Bilateral contracting is generally beneficial as it supports competitive investment to meet resource adequacy goals 
and provides risk mitigation for supply and demand-side market participants. See Meeting the Challenge of Resource 
Adequacy in Regional Transmission Organization and Independent System Operator Regions, Post-Technical 
Conference Comments of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket No. AD25-7-000, at 5-9 (July 7, 2025).  
12 In its recent whitepaper on the future of its markets, PJM stressed the importance of bilateral contracting for retail 
ratepayer loads through their Load Serving Entities (LSEs) and Electric Distribution Companies (EDCs).  PJM 
suggested this could be done either through an individual LSE hedging requirement or through a PJM-administered, 
long-term procurement, such as a tiered, multi-year capacity market.  See Powering Reliability Through Market 
Design, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (May 6, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-
notices/special-reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-market-design.pdf.

8 
 
complicated matters sometimes cannot be resolved and formal proceedings are initiated at the 
Commission.  In addition to working through these disputes itself, based on the record submitted 
by the parties (as it typically does), the Commission should be more expansive in its use of 
settlement proceedings, providing guidance as to what it would find (un)acceptable, imposing tight 
deadlines on discussions (which can motivate parties to compromise), and encouraging settlement 
judges to actively engage in the process and discussions.13  This has worked well in the past.  The 
original Reliability Pricing Model mechanism was developed as part of a Commission settlement 
process that was initiated and shaped by a prior Commission “guidance” order.14  Cost allocation 
issues in the wake of the GreenHat default also were resolved by settlement,15 and numerous PJM-
related complaints filed in the wake of Winter Storm Elliott were resolved through a Commission-
ordered expedited settlement process.16 
The Commission also should consider more frequent use of designating non-decisional 
Commission staff on contentious policy matters.  Non-decisional Commission staff can help PJM, 
the states and stakeholders to better understand Commission policy guidance and increase the 
likelihood that the resolution of conflicts or rule changes are ultimately found by the Commission 
to be just and reasonable.  For instance, non-decisional staff played a key role in supporting PJM 
stakeholders when responding to Commission directed changes to PJM’s capacity market (i.e., 
Minimum Offer Price Rule).17  
 
13 A Commission Policy Statement could lay out how the Commission will make use of such mechanism, including if 
requested by the parties. 
14 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 115 FERC ¶ 61,079, at P 176 (2006) (Initial Order on Reliability Pricing 
Model).   
15 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 167 FERC ¶ 61,209, at PP 28-29 (2019). 
16 See Essential Power OPP, LLC, 183 FERC ¶ 61,163, at P 17 (2023). 
17 See Calpine Corp. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Notice of Designation of Commission Staff as Non-Decisional, 
Docket Nos. EL16-49-000, et al. (July 17, 2018); Calpine Corp. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 163 FERC ¶ 61,236 
(2018).

9 
 
C. PJM’s Role: Using its Stakeholder Processes and Governance Mechanisms to 
Address System Needs in a Timely and Efficient Manner 
In Constellation’s experience, many of the complaints about PJM’s stakeholder process 
and its governance mechanisms are, in actuality, disagreements with PJM about its decisions to 
take, defer, or decline a particular action combined with a perception that competing views have 
not been adequately considered.  The Commission’s goal cannot be for PJM to always agree or 
take unwavering direction from a particular entity or group of entities.  That would be inconsistent 
with the core independence principle of Order No. 2000, which the Commission enforces in order 
to ensure that each RTO has “a decisionmaking process that is independent of control by any 
market participant or class of participants.”18  The same is true of states, which should participate 
extensively in RTO processes and, as discussed above, have the resources and organizational 
structures to do so.  While improvements are needed in PJM to ensure that the views of states (as 
well as other stakeholders) are fully considered, it does not follow that states need or should be 
given filing rights under section 205 of the FPA or decisional control over PJM leadership.   
1. PJM Leadership Matters Most 
Whether an issue is raised for consideration by a stakeholder or PJM, PJM sets the agenda 
for its standing committees and task forces, where most of the substantive work is done.  It is 
PJM’s responsibility, then, to use its stakeholder process to drive to decisions instead of delay. 
Stakeholders look to PJM to determine when an issue has been fully vetted, opportunities for 
collaboration or compromise have been exhausted, and it is time for PJM or stakeholders to move 
 
18 Regional Transmission Organizations, Order No. 2000, 89 FERC ¶ 61,285, at slip op. 194 (1999), order on reh’g, 
Order No. 2000-A, 90 FERC ¶ 61,201 (2000), petitions for review dismissed sub nom. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 v. 
FERC, 272 F.3d 607 (D.C. Cir. 2001); see Duquesne Light Co., 189 FERC ¶ 61,181, at PP 24-25, 43-47 (2024), 
order on reh’g, 192 FERC ¶ 61,051, at PP 36-40 (2025) (Commission reiterating the importance of PJM 
independence), aff’d sub nom. PJM Transmission Owners v. FERC, Nos. 25-1064, 25-1100, 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 
16255 (D.C. Cir. June 5, 2026).

10 
 
forward with a decision.  Undoubtedly, PJM has a difficult job balancing competing interests with 
respect to prioritization, timing, information, transparency, and direction, and there will always be 
stakeholders who would like additional time to discuss an issue or additional information before 
making a decision, sometimes with the intent of delaying a resolution of an issue rather than 
reaching consensus.  PJM’s leadership can reduce gridlock by making decisions on a timely basis, 
communicating its decisions clearly, explaining its views of alternative positions, and sticking with 
its decisions through execution and over time.   
When PJM strikes the balance right, working collaboratively with stakeholders, it can 
successfully and timely address some of the system’s most pressing needs.  For example, the 
Interconnection Process Reform Task Force was able, in the span of roughly one year, to develop 
both significant reforms to the PJM interconnection process and a transition mechanism to address 
the backlog of existing interconnection requests.  Guided by clear goals and timeframes from PJM, 
stakeholders were able to consider a range of PJM and stakeholder proposed solutions, agree on a 
package of reforms, and file that package at the Commission.19  This is how the stakeholder process 
should work. 
Without clear guidance from PJM, the stakeholder process can instead flounder. For 
example, the Reserve Certainty Senior Task Force began its work in 2023 with a dauntingly long 
project plan timeline, has had numerous restarts as PJM has revised its deliverables, has failed to 
file one set of reforms that PJM deemed necessary, and is stumbling toward the finish line where 
it is unclear that any proposal will receive sector-weighted majority support.  Even initiatives 
designed to be accelerated can, without PJM leadership, fail to meet their intended goals.  Such 
 
19 See Tariff Revisions for Interconnection Process Reform of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER22-2110-
000, at 2, 13 (June 14, 2022), accepted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 61,162 (2022), order on reh’g, 
184 FERC ¶ 61,006 (2023), aff’d sub nom. Hecate Energy LLC v. FERC, 126 F.4th 660 (2025).

11 
 
was the case with last year’s Critical Issue Fast Path (CIFP)-Large Load Addition stakeholder 
process which, after months of deliberation, led to a second CIFP process instead of a decision on 
issues that had been vetted fully. 
2. Who Has Section 205 Filing Rights Is a Red Herring 
Some nevertheless argue that PJM’s section 205 rights should be expanded, pointing to a 
lack of Member endorsement leading to gridlock.  As discussed above, PJM already has section 
205 filing rights over resource adequacy, generator retirements and replacements, and capacity 
market rule changes which have been the most contentious issues in PJM particularly for the states.  
Dissatisfaction over PJM’s actions and inactions on these issues has more to do with how PJM is 
addressing (or not) feedback received than who has the right to propose a rule change under 
section 205.  And while it is true that PJM needs Member endorsement to file an energy market 
rule change under section 205, the lack of stakeholder approval has not stopped PJM in the past 
from proceeding with filings under section 206 when its leadership concluded that a change was 
necessary despite stakeholders not reaching the consensus necessary for PJM to file under section 
205.20 
Others argue that states should be given section 205 filing rights, but that would be 
inconsistent with the very structure of the Federal Power Act.  Utilities providing jurisdictional 
service have filing rights, and the Commission reviews proposed changes to ensure they are just 
and reasonable.  The same is true for state regulation of utilities.  If either the Commission or a 
state commission desires to change a tariff or market rule, it can initiate its own proceeding to 
investigate if that change is needed.  It would be unreasonable to give states more authority over 
 
20 See supra note 4.

12 
 
filings made by Commission-jurisdictional RTOs than the Commission itself has, or more than 
states have over their own utilities.21   
If the Commission nonetheless believes that something has changed that now renders 
PJM’s existing filing rights over market rules unjust, unreasonable and unduly preferential, then it 
is generators who should receive additional authority to expedite section 205 filings proposing 
changes to those rules.  Generators are the only entities providing capacity, energy, and related 
jurisdictional services under the FPA.  To the extent generators ceded any of their rights under 
section 205 in agreeing to participate in PJM, they cannot be forced to further cede those rights 
through other changes to the filing rights structure in PJM.22   
3. Board Member Selection Must Remain Independent 
Finally, it is essential that PJM’s Board member selection process remain independent of 
undue influence from any particular interest.23  PJM’s existing selection process is consistent with 
Commission precedent and welcomes input, including potential nominees, from all interested 
parties.24  This is a healthy process that is fair to all Members and is consistent with approaches 
used in other regions.  
 
21 Some incorrectly point to “jump ball” rights in New England as an example of states having section 205 filing 
rights.  In reality, those “jump ball” rights are held by the New England Power Pool, which is an association of 
representatives from six sectors of the electricity industry: generators, suppliers, transmission owners or utilities, end 
users, publicly owned entities, and alternative resources. See Corporate Governance, ISO New England Inc., 
https://www.iso-ne.com/about/corporate-governance. In MISO and SPP, states have limited rights to require or 
otherwise request the RTO to submit section 205 filings addressing resource adequacy and transmission cost 
allocation.  That authority is tailored to the particular regulatory structures of those regions, which are dominated by 
vertically integrated utilities with states engaging regularly in integrated resource planning. 
22 With respect to substantive capacity market matters, PJM only has authority to make filings under section 205 to 
the extent such authority has been contracted to it.  But as noted, PJM cannot force those providing jurisdictional 
services to provide PJM with even more of their section 205 rights. 
23 See supra note 19. 
24 PJM Nominating Committee offers the opportunity for any interested person to submit candidates directly to an 
independent consultant (currently, Korn Ferry International).  See Nominating Committee, PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C., https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/committees/nc; Operating Agreement §§ 7.1-7.2.

13 
 
Some states in PJM have requested a more formal role in Board member selections.  Giving 
any group, whether states or anyone else, an outsized role in Board member selection could 
undermine the independence of the Board and PJM as an organization.  Instead, states can and 
should make their views known about potential Board members by taking advantage of existing 
opportunities to engage.  This could include coordinating efforts by developing a list of suggested 
nominees, perhaps through OPSI or through the formation of nomination advisory group 
consisting of state-designated representatives.   
Relatedly, it is important that the Board is immune from political pressure and has all the 
information it needs in making decisions.  To ensure Board independence is maintained, PJM 
stakeholders and the Commission should evaluate whether Board terms should be lengthened, and 
whether substantive criteria should be adopted for removing Board members, to promote well-
informed Board decisions that are immune from political influence.  In addition, to support the 
Board’s consideration of complicated policy decisions, the Board should be given access to input 
from third-party market experts when complex technical matters are being considered.25 
II. 
CONCLUSION 
Thank you for the opportunity to address the Commission regarding potential PJM 
governance reforms.  Constellation looks forward to working with the Commission, PJM, its 
stakeholders, and that states as we evaluate and implement improvements to existing processes to 
make participation more effective while supporting PJM’s leadership and independence.   
 
July 14, 2026 
 
25 Improvements could also include returning the Liaison Committee meetings to being entirely in-person and 
separate from the Annual Meeting and/or adding networking receptions at each Board meeting where there isn’t a 
Liaison Committee meeting.
